transcript.text:
Operator
Good day, and welcome to the Molecular Partners First Half 2024 Results Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note today's event is being recorded.
I'd now like to turn the conference over to Seth Lewis, Senior Vice President, Investor Relations. Please go ahead.
Seth D. Lewis
Vice President
Thanks, Rocco. Good morning and good afternoon, everyone. Welcome to the Molecular Partners First Half 2024 Results Call. My name is Seth Lewis, Senior Vice President of Investor Relations, and I'm joined this morning by Patrick Amstutz, and Philippe Legenne, Chief Medical Officer; Dani Steiner, Senior Vice President, Research and Technology; and Robert Hendriks, Senior Vice President of Finance.
Management will take a few minutes to make brief remarks, and then we will open up for a question-and-answer period. If you have not had a chance to review the H1 press release, please feel free to do so on our website, www.molecularpartners.com.
Also on the website is today's updated presentation, which management may refer to in speaking or answering your questions. As a reminder, today's call is being recorded. Today's discussion and presentation will contain certain forward-looking statements. based on the information available to molecular partners as of the date of this release, and actual results may differ materially from what is discussed today.
With that, I'm happy to turn the call over to Patrick Amstutz, CEO, to review the highlights and outlook for the company. Please go ahead.
Patrick Amstutz
Co-Founder, CEO, Member of Management Board & Director
Thanks, Seth, for the nice introduction, and a very warm welcome from my side to everyone on the call, investors, analysts and people interested in our update. As Seth alluded to, we have the slides on our home page. And what we will do is not go through every slide, but really jump to the highlights. We will say which slide number we are on and go rather fast that we have more time in the end to answer your question.
With that, I will jump to Slide #5, the corporate highlights of the first half of 2024. The first half was really active. We progressed a lot of programs, and I will start with CD33, where we have great progress. We have reached the top dose. And despite not reaching the optimal exposure or concentration due to half-life and target-mediated drug disposition, we see activity, and Philippe will allude to that. And we also see a way forward to those higher and more frequent. On the staying with the immune cell engager front, I go to [indiscernible], where we have updated the molecule presented at EHA. And this is a cKIT targeting switch molecule, a very innovative way of killing HSCTs and LSEs and best applied in for stem cell conditioning.
On 317, that's why we have finalized the clinical trial for our tumor-localized CD40 agonist, we have a nice safety profile, and we can conclude biological proof-of-concept and are looking into combination settings going forward. And I do end with [indiscernible] the most exciting part, which is the radio DARPins, where with MP0712, we have a first candidate that the DLL3 targeting DARPin, optimized for low kidney uptake and high tumor accumulation and that is in collaboration with Orano Med where we struck a strategic alliance earlier in the year to work together on targeting net-based radio isotopes by DARPins. And we call that a strategic collaboration as we believe, lead access circumvents keep limitations of other isotopes including supply, and Dani can speak a bit more about that.
On the operating side, we are in a strong financial position with CHF 159 million in cash and that puts our runway into 2027, which is a bit further than we had so far on our chart.
Before handing over to Philippe, I go to the slide, I think it's now Number 6, where I have a really personal nice announcement to make. I'm very happy about it. which is that Philippe Legenne has been promoted to full Chief Medic, after serving a year in that role as Acting Chief Medic. And he really deserves this role, on the one hand, by impressive recruitment. I mean our trials, the cohorts were full when they were opened, and the execution was flawless. And [indiscernible] in my CEO of biotechs, we know how important that is. That's where you build all the credibility. That's where you build all the value. So big thanks to Philippe and his team for that, that's just excellent execution. And that is only possible because Philippe has a gift to engage investigators into our trial. So they think of our trials for us. They understand the importance, and he's really a strong networker there. And it doesn't really end on the investigator side. It includes the KOLs that he brings into review our data, help us on the next steps, and that's also how we came about how to move forward on 533 with the top global experts in the room.
Given that he is not only an AML specialist, but he has a really broad understanding of tumors. He can apply that also to our earlier pipeline of DLL3 radiotherapy. So in that sense, he is in a perfect position to apply his knowledge, skills and with his team bring forward the molecules in our pipeline and [indiscernible] profits also from the industry background with Novartis, GSK and Amgen. And as I just pointed out, it's also his personal dedication, passion, his team leadership and the way he works, not only with the KOLs, but also with us and his team is inspiring every day. And it's a great pleasure to have he as full Chief Medic now, and it's also a great pleasure to give you the word to give us an update on the 533 molecule.
Daniel Steiner
Senior Vice President of Research
Thanks, Patrick. I'm glad it's audio and not video or otherwise, you would see blushing. But I want to thank before this. And again, it's a honor to be with this MP team and to help and lead and contribute to push our programs to the clinic and having the fortune to be able to reach and work with the worldwide experts. So I will want to give you fairly quickly, quick mode, an update on the 533. And basically, in my few minutes here, I will refer mainly to the Slide #14. We can spend more time later on to go through Q&A, come back to any slides where there will be questions, but basically, I want to give you a summary and outlook of where we are.
So on that Slide 14, basically, I would like -- I have mainly 4 points of updates on the program. First of all is that we are reporting here of [indiscernible], and as we speak, we are [indiscernible] 7 now. But basically, we have seen an ongoing and very, very steady engagement from the PITs, and basically, there is very good dynamics on this team -- on this trial recruitments from the very beginning up to now.
What have we observed? We have observed first is that an acceptable safety profile, a manageable safety profile with mainly the IRR and CRS as we expected on the T-cell engager. And we see them basically in the first cycle and rapid decrease in second cycle onwards. We've seen indisputable activity, reduction in myeloblast on half of the patient population recruited, and on 25%, more than 50% reduction in those [indiscernible]. And that translates into [indiscernible] responses from with 1 responder per cohort from BR 3, 4, 5 and 6. So individual activity yes. But in a way, we need to have more than that to be completely satisfied and to qualify that we would unlock the potential of that compound.
And when we observed in greater detail, in fact, we realized that we still have to improve the exposure of the product. In fact, we need to increase that exposure and have it more durable in order to increase the response rate, the depth of response and the durability, and therefore, we are further amending the protocol for, again, a higher and more [indiscernible] dosing, especially in the first weeks to densify this exporter. And we will share later this year at the end and also in, especially in the next year 2025 results from those [indiscernible]. So obviously, we will review those results very carefully to see whether we can truly gate the future developments and move into the expansion and Phase II steps.
So that's my update. And again, very glad to go into more detail in the Q&A part of the discussion of the session.
Patrick Amstutz
Co-Founder, CEO, Member of Management Board & Director
Thanks, Philippe. And with that, I will then hand over to an update from on the radio side of Dani Steiner, who is with his colleagues leading that effort.
Daniel Steiner
Senior Vice President of Research
Thanks, Patrick. So happy to guide you through this update top line update on the radio IP therapy with the first candidate, as Patrick already introduced, MP0712, the first program, we're moving towards the clinic. So for those of you who are on this slide, I'm jumping now to Slide #25. And as I said, top line update there, and I'm super proud about the great progress the team has made to successfully move the RTT platform to profile with an attractive biodistribution profile in terms of tumor kidney to blood ratios. And we can dive into Q&A way more into the details if you're interested AND-YOU-HAVE questions. So here, the date on MP0712, which has been selected as the lead candidate for targeted LED212 DLL3 program has been presented at [indiscernible], and it really showcased the strength of the platform that we have been establishing. And of course, the IND-enabling activities are now ongoing with Orano Med and additional clinical data is expected in 2025.
So as I've been mentioning, super excited what the team has achieved here and even more excited about the opportunities that this all opens up. So of course, we are advancing 712 and the current pipeline together with Orano Med, which we see is very strong and committed collaboration partner, but also with Novartis where we have an ongoing collaboration since the start of our activities in the radioligand space. And we are evolving and expanding the platform for next differentiated RGT programs. And this is what I'm looking for most, and I'm going to tell you a bit more about this on the next slide. So if you move to Slide 26.
So this is just an initial, I'd say, glimpse or preview of how we are thinking about leveraging the DARPin properties to really build differentiated RDT and RDT portfolio and RDT candidate with a high level of differentiation. So if you look at the top panel of the slide, for me, this is just 2 examples then there is more, and we're going to tell you more about this in the months and future to come. These are 2 examples of how we are thinking about targeting proteins, tumor targets, which are difficult to address with classical, I say, radioligands in the sense of low molecular or peptides. And one class, the piece on the left-hand side is like where you have a high amount of soluble antigen, which is interfering [indiscernible] solid antigen, which is interfering tumor uptake, and there we found an approach to target specifically the membrane down for only that we're building on the selectivity and the binding properties of the DARPin. And on the right-hand side, you see in other clouds of targets we are heavily investing to is like targets with have [indiscernible] with high identity on healthy cells, where you, by using the selectivity of DARPin, can really tumor specifically DARPin by only recognizing this specific form. And of course, on the other side, and that's at the lower part of the slide, we are building on the deep expertise we have in making multi-specific molecules here in the context of having a broader and more homogeneous tumor distribution to address heterogeneity, which we believe is especially in the context of short-range alpha emitting particles, a key aspect to consider. And there, and that's what we see on the left-hand side, we are not thinking mainly about classical multispecifics as they are used in our IO project.
It's really more building on the concept of having 2 [indiscernible] in 1 single DARPin domain, which we call 2 in 1, which keeps the size of the molecule small by maintaining all the binding properties of DARPin. So this is something just a teaser in what to come in the next 12 months. Looking very much forward to give you more details on that, starting to present on those approaches on conferences at is just like giving you a bit of an outlook of what we are up for. And with this, I would like to hand over to Robert to give you insights into our financials forecast.
Robert Hendriks
Vice President of Finance
Thank you, Dani, and prior speakers. Before we move to the summary and a Q&A, I will brief you guide you through the financial highlights and the key figures and the updated guidance for this year. My name is Robert Hendriks, and I'm the SVP of Finance here at MP. The numbers, I will show are stated in million swiss francs, and full detail of the financials is available on the website and on other means. If I move to Slide 28 with the highlights. I'd like to focus firstly on our cash position. We ended last year with around CHF 187 million. And by the end of June, we are at CHF 159 million. So that's a cash burn of CHF 28 million, in line with our expectations.
If we take us to a full year 12 months running, the burn is CHF 59 million. We had no additional cash coming in from collaborations in '24.
With that, moving on to the updated guidance for the full year. We are now guiding our operating expenses to end up in the CHF 65 million to CHF 75 million range. This is a reduction from the previous guidance, largely based on what we see in our actuals at the moment and the current expectations we have on the development of the cost and the workforce. We will not guide on revenue. And for clarity, this guidance is, as always, subject to the progress and changes of our pipeline.
Thirdly, following also from the updated guidance is our runway. We are now feeling comfortable to say that we are funded into '27, which is a small change from late '26, which we had guided on before. We do feel that this runway and the cash that we have at the moment does put us in a privileged position in the industry. It will allow us to reach the milestones as presented by my colleagues, in particular, the funds that we [indiscernible] [ 4533 ], as indicated by Philippe, as well as the further progression of the radio pipeline.
We then turn over to the next slide, I'll briefly show comparison with last year for 6 months running. Overall, the results, you can see are in a pretty similar range. Revenue was slightly up as well as operating expenses, resulting in an almost equal operating result. Financial results was driven in the first 6 months by a positive exchange impact on our cash position as well as an increase in the interest income on the same balances.
The revenue that we show continues to be driven out in Novartis radioligand contract collaboration and the focus on operating expenses. And R&D expenses are up a bit. G&A expenses came down a bit. On SG&A, we were able to see a reduction in our D&O insurance expense. When looking at R&D, in the first 6 months of '24, in comparison to last year, we did invest more in drug product in the dose escalation trials for 533 as indicated by Philippe. We also were able to increase our investments in the overall platform and the radio space and a few reductions we saw on, for instance, 317 and some legacy programs. We are and do remain diligent and careful in looking at our expenses. We feel that we are cost effective, on a tight ship that remains on course for us to deliver on the promises. In combination, I think that these numbers continue to show the strong financial base entering into the second half that will allow us to keep investing in the pipeline. Thank you for your attention. Any questions, happy to take them in the Q&A. And now I hand back to Patrick.
Patrick Amstutz
Co-Founder, CEO, Member of Management Board & Director
Thanks, Robert. Thanks, Dani. Thanks, Philippe. Thanks, Seth. And before turning to questions, let me quickly summarize. I'm on Slide 34, which is the outlook on the upcoming milestones. 533, we heard, we're testing both higher and more frequent dosing to come to a conclusion on the potential of this molecule, where we will update in 2025. Switch DARPin. we are in animal trials. We'll summarize the data, present and then define next development step for that molecule. 317, the Phase I is completed. We are in discussions with investigators to investigator-initiated trials for that. We don't plan to invest heavily ourselves, but we would like to understand more on 317 what combination trials could help. And there's a good means to test that. And last, but not least, obviously, the radio franchise where [ 212 ] going into clinics next year. I'm also very excited, as Dani pointed out, the differentiated DARPin programs, where we will update our portfolio and give you a insight how we are thinking about those programs and how clinical value can then build in the future. And obviously, we're not doing that alone. We're working with Novartis and especially also with Orano Med, where we are excited to be working with the leader in the lead-based isotope field.
As Robert said, we're running a tight ship. So the cash runway is now into 2027. And I think with really the effectiveness of our research and development engine, it puts us on course to find many important programs. many updates to come and a really exciting year ahead of us.
Before moving on to Q&A, I would like to take the opportunity to, first of all, thank the people here with me in the room, my speakers, but also all other coworkers at Molecular Partners. We are partners, we're coworkers, we're a team. And what we present you today is really the hard work of a whole company coming together and executing and debating and thinking and positioning our DARPin work.
I would also like to extend the thanks to our partners, Novartis and Orano Med, but also our academic partners that we have. And obviously, also our investigators and KOLs who are using our molecules or applying the molecules in the clinic. And there, my last thanks goes to all the patients in our trials and their families because without them, this would not be possible. That leads me back to the key purpose of our company. We're all here today to make drugs that matter. And with that, I would close the presentation and open for your questions. Thanks.
Operator
[Operator Instructions] And today's first question comes from Daina Graybosch with Leerink Parkers.
Daina Michelle Graybosch
MD & Senior Research Analyst, SVB Leerink LLC, Research Division
I have one back on MP0533. I love your thoughts on how you're thinking about escalating now the higher doses and the trade-off between efficacy and tox. And I wonder, as you get to these higher doses, do you expect to bind and single antigen expressing tumor cells or normal cells? And what specific toxs are you looking for that might indicate that you're actually at such a high dose that you no longer have the advantageous therapeutic window of needing to buying multiple antigens? So basically, what are you looking for in the clinical signal to balance that tox and efficacy as you go higher?
Patrick Amstutz
Co-Founder, CEO, Member of Management Board & Director
I can lead in as maybe more the generalist view and then I'll hand over to Philippe for a more expert view. I think, first of all, why are we going to higher doses, and it was an observation also by our KOLs when we looked at the data is that we have the dose [indiscernible], where we have an induction at a very low dose, and then we go up and that was to manage the safety. And so we start at a low dose and then over the first 20 days, we had injections with always higher doses. And they realized that with maybe a bit faster PK than expected and maybe also more target mediated drug deposition than expected, we were not getting the exposure that we were hoping for and we were rather underdosing. So the dose intensification now is that we will give more higher doses, but maybe not even higher top doses, but just go faster to the full dose and then dose more frequent.
The side effect that we have seen so far are IRRs in CRS, which is really the T-cell activation. So far, I don't think we have seen target dependent toxicities, and Philippe can talk about that.
Now if the patients will tolerate this intensification, that's what we have to explore, there is -- and maybe there will even be a lower dose, but more frequent dose that will actually end up being the most efficacious dose in the beginning. We also know that once the disease is under control, we cannot dose every 2, 3 days. That's not possible and also not practical. So then we'll go back to the weekly dosing scheme at that point in time. So that's why we're talking about the dose intensification in the early weeks and then back to weekly. Hopefully, that's then enough once the disease is under control, and we also [indiscernible] the target mediated drug at position anymore. So Philippe, maybe you can explain a bit more. And there's also some slides in our deck where we show that especially the low -- patients with low disease burden profited more because, obviously, they also have maybe a bit less of those problems, and there was just enough drug to keep the disease under control. Philippe?
Philippe Legenne
Interim Chief Medical Officer
So thanks to you had a couple of complements to what Patrick just said. First of all, again, we have seen good tolerability, manageable toxicity up to now and mainly CRS with very little pattern beyond that dose CRS IRR. So -- and we've been carefully looking, for example, at cytopenia or neutropenia, which could be expected, which we have seen on some other programs. So we want to identify, as Patrick said. Why? Because we see a higher zinc for target-mediated disposition than we had anticipated. And so we want to -- and also because it's safe so far, we think we can go quicker high. So we put that in place. We [indiscernible] what will be the exact impact on the half-life, but we may still have significant zinc. And that's why we do not anticipate so far too much drug accumulation.
Therefore, we do not think that we would get much more on target toxicity and -- but we will be especially monitoring the cytopenia. So that's the 1 we will be looking at mostly for the moment.
Daina Michelle Graybosch
MD & Senior Research Analyst, SVB Leerink LLC, Research Division
Can I ask a follow-up then? So as you have modeled out the PK and the drug-mediated clearance, [indiscernible] specific dose, what sort of dose level do you expect [indiscernible] optimize your activity then, the exposure based on your preclinical model?
Philippe Legenne
Interim Chief Medical Officer
Basically, we are ready and part of the amendment, which we are currently putting in allows for a few higher due escalation. So not doesn't, but a few higher dose escalation. And again, counting a lot on the densification, even more than higher than the dose increase. So that's basically -- we want to modify the exposure. We are not very far from where we would be hoping to be in terms of CMAX, but we need to work on the C trough a longer exporter or at least identifying all those things, which we already see, but want to really harmonize, if I may say.
Patrick Amstutz
Co-Founder, CEO, Member of Management Board & Director
So Philippe, is it fair to say from the modeling we saw that was just CMAX increase we will not reach what we need. That's why we need to intensify with more dose?
Philippe Legenne
Interim Chief Medical Officer
Yes. We see, again, on one hand, we are reassured and the experts with us are reassured that we see there is an impact on the tumors. There is an impact on the [indiscernible]. We really hit them. But we think it's not long-lasting enough, it's disappearing too quickly, and we need to modify that trend. So to gain that increase in effects and especially the duration of the effect.
Operator
And our next question today comes from Richard Vosser at JPMorgan.
Richard Vosser
Senior Analyst
Maybe another one on 0533. Just back on that I suppose, the dose intensifying after a period of time. If you then go to -- back to weekly dosing, are you going to have enough drug on board to maintain the response? How should we think about that, will be the first question?
Philippe Legenne
Interim Chief Medical Officer
Very good question. You should join us for our protocol discussion. But we hope is that we are going to debulk, if I may say, or reduce the tumor magnitude, tumor burden, because we see again -- we see that we have more responses in the lower tumor burden than in the higher. So we want to -- and we hope that when we are there, then we may need less because there could be some less of a sync. So that's one aspect. We are still discussing, in fact, in terms of -- we also want to avoid by design having chronic exposure because we are also conscious of that concept of a T-cell exhaustion. So we would want to be continuous all the time. Then the question is how little is enough?
And so we are, in fact, discussing [indiscernible] one day of reexposure in that maintenance phase or more than one day, but we know that it will not be continuous, and it will be a short time, too. So we are just finalizing that discussion as we speak, but very, very close to finalize and submit.
Operator
And our next question comes from Sebastiaan van der Schoot with Kempen.
Sebastiaan van der Schoot
Analyst
Regarding the radio DARPin, can you remind us when the clinical trial is supposed to start? And can you also give some insight into what the clinical trial design will be, how you are thinking about the different steps, and when we can see first data for the DARPin when you get to the less payload?
Patrick Amstutz
Co-Founder, CEO, Member of Management Board & Director
Yes. So I can give you a rough outline. We have defined the candidates. We are now of production. It's going to be GMP production. Then we will be working with Orano Med for the net payload. So we are expecting clinical entry next year second half. So first half is not possible. And then we have guided that we are expecting to have first data and the data will not be efficacy or safety, it will be images, where we can follow the molecule. That is the beauty of this setup where we can create an image after dosing and see where the drug is. And I think from the image, we can do some predictions. I mean, is it less in the kidney, more indicate, more in the tumor, but the safety and efficacy will obviously follow later.
Now I'll be happy to hand over to the experts, and Philippe on the clinical side. And I think the good thing is the image is actually available rather short after dosing. So you don't have to wait for 3 months for the pictures, you actually can get them rather fast. That's why clinical entry and initial data are rather close together. Philippe?
Philippe Legenne
Interim Chief Medical Officer
Thanks for that. So again, we want to very quickly or quickly after patients are included. They will be imaged for biodistribution and dosimetry. And then on the heels of that, obviously, those escalations start. So I just also want to make sure this -- we're envisioning a single trial, which will have those 2 steps. But again, the images come first and then therapeutic comes in. So that -- and obviously, we would want to go what we are planning to do for the moment. is to include patients with small cell lung cancer mainly. And depending on the signal that we get, we'll expand in potentially the prostate, neuroendocrine, but I think it's a bit difficult to integrate both subpopulation at the very start.
Operator
[Operator Instructions] Our next question comes from Michael Nedelcovych with TD Cowen.
Michael Thomas Nedelcovych
Research Associate, Cowen and Company, LLC, Research Division
I have another follow-up on 0533, and this is maybe a slightly different version of a question that was already asked. But do you all have a CMAX or an exposure level in mind at which you would expect activity or at least more activity than you've seen and are aiming for that level? Or are you approaching this more empirically in trying to raise the dose and the dose frequency and the dose regimen and just waiting to see what you see? So that's the first question.
And then I have to admit that the language around this program is a little bit ominous in the slides. If we learn in about a year that you have discontinued this program, what do you think will be the most likely reason? Would it be because your hypothesis has not panned out? Or would it be that you have so many other compelling opportunities that resource allocation has to come first and you'll pursue those other opportunities? And I realize that's not the fairest hypothetical, but I'm just curious where your minds are at at the moment.
Patrick Amstutz
Co-Founder, CEO, Member of Management Board & Director
Maybe Philippe can take the first, and I'll take the next one.
Seth D. Lewis
Vice President
Congratulations on your promotion, Philippe. Please go ahead.
Philippe Legenne
Interim Chief Medical Officer
But very good question again on the CMAX and or model. Obviously, we model, and we think that we are not the in terms of CMAX from where we were we wanted to do, and we see activity. So it's more about we see too much too quickly disappearance of the drug. That's why we need to change, evolve our...
Patrick Amstutz
Co-Founder, CEO, Member of Management Board & Director
Dosing pattern.
Philippe Legenne
Interim Chief Medical Officer
Dosing pattern, our scheme of administration to to really, let's say, have a more, again, dense approach during that first phase. So we are not very far, and we still think we can go a bit higher, and we'd like to tease that out. Again, we can do this because it has been safe up to now or safe enough. But it will be much -- it will be more about looking at the shape of that exposure curve more than the CMAX. And again, we'll have a heavy focus on the trough because we need to have more time with higher than mean expected exposure during that time.
Patrick Amstutz
Co-Founder, CEO, Member of Management Board & Director
And maybe just kind of -- obviously, I'm not a medic, but a bit more of the layman's view and please apologize if it is too crude, but this disease progresses very fast. If you cannot control the patient in the first days even, you are behind the disease. And if you look at the data that we also did show, I think, on Slide 12, you see we have some impact and then just the disease takes off. And so it's very important that we not only -- and I think it's more the trough that we actually give the dose. And we give it also faster just to get the drug more chance to actually act before it's too late. And I would -- and you were asking about the empiricism of it. I personally was surprised that we saw, let's say, no dose response in the sense that we had patients in almost all those cohorts that responded, but we don't see it those response in that sense. We see activity in patients that have low disease burden. And maybe that's also why we just need to tease that out and see if we can expand that activity to more patients by, what we call, intensifying the dose.
And we will have a [indiscernible] where you then can see what those we have now, and it is definitely less than we would like. And I think that was the modeling, call it, a bit surprised that we saw less drug in circulation, and that's what we are correcting for based on also some responses we save in despite the low exposure.
I'll now take the other part of the question, which is sort of what to expect? And it was a good discussion with our investigators, and there is just a high medical need. And everyone in the room, the KOLs on the trial, but also those not on the trials said we should really test this. As we have activity, there is a need there and the higher dosing is just what -- just jumps into the eye when you saw the data that we have. So I think there is almost an ethical imperative for us to test this. At the same time, outcome, we will see what it is.
The good thing, and I'll turn almost your question around is we have options. We don't have to progress this one if the radio franchise works well, means not that we would stop it for no reason, but it puts a clear bar that we can put out there and say, if we don't reach 20 or even 30 plus response rate, if we don't have the duration of 3, 6, maybe 9 months, that's just not going to be good enough and that's going to be a clinical response. I mean that's what we're looking for. It won't be the cost is more or less the same as we always had. I mean that's what would allow you to move forward into Phase II/registrational trial. And we can just be very clean about that. I don't think it will just go away. So we will [indiscernible] update on the data. We want to update on the data and our reasoning why we would stop it or not.
So -- but I do say that the idea that we have options, obviously, is a good one. And the more competition there is for the cash we have, it's a good sign for the company.
Operator
And our next question is a follow-up from Richard Vosser at JPMorgan.
Richard Vosser
Senior Analyst
It was back on the radio DARPin side of things. Just maybe an update on Novartis partnership as much as you can give just where we are with that one? How that's progressing relative to 0712, and when we might see something from that side of the collaboration?
Patrick Amstutz
Co-Founder, CEO, Member of Management Board & Director
Maybe Dani can give a short update, and maybe just frame that, obviously, in our pipeline, our compounds are like, we have 5 and they're all 5 high priority. And in the Novartis' pipeline, they're close to 30 compounds and that explains maybe a bit less speed. But maybe over to Dani to explain how we are progressing our pipeline, and why we think we are faster and how Novartis is going forward?
